title: India's Anaemia Programme Has Ambition but No New Outcome Data
excerpt: NFHS-6 dropped haemoglobin entirely, leaving Anaemia Mukt Bharat judged on tablets distributed rather than blood levels improved since 2019-21.
body:
• The last national survey with anaemia data, NFHS-5 (2019-21), found 67.1% of children aged 6-59 months and 57% of women aged 15-49 were anaemic.
  • NFHS-6 fact sheets for 2023-24, released in May 2026, contain no haemoglobin estimates at all, leaving the Anaemia Mukt Bharat programme without a current national outcome measure.
  • Officials say finger-prick capillary testing overstated anaemia; a venous-blood survey, SAMPADA/DABS-I, is meant to replace it, but its results cannot be directly compared with the old series.
  • Reader check: if you are pregnant or caring for a child under five in India, ask for a haemoglobin test at your local health facility — programme inputs such as iron tablets distributed do not tell you your own level.

India runs one of the world's largest programmes against anaemia and currently has no new national data to show whether it is working. The National Family Health Survey's sixth round, NFHS-6, whose fact sheets for 2023-24 were released in May 2026, includes body mass index, blood pressure and blood glucose. It does not include haemoglobin, the measurement used to estimate anaemia, as ApDirect's review of the fact sheets sets out. For the first time in the survey series, there is no fresh NFHS anaemia estimate for women or young children.

The last picture, in absolute numbers

The most recent comparable national figures are from NFHS-5, conducted in 2019-21. It found anaemia in 67.1% of children aged six to 59 months, up from 58.6% in NFHS-4. Among women aged 15 to 49, prevalence was about 57%, up from 53.1%. Among pregnant women it was 52.2%, up from 50.4%, according to the NFHS-5 figures summarised by Health and Family. In plain terms, at last measurement more than two in three toddlers and more than one in two women of reproductive age in India were anaemic.

The burden is not evenly spread. The same summary cites Assam, where 65.9% of women and 68.4% of children had low haemoglobin, and notes rural rates exceed urban rates in almost all states. Globally, the World Health Organization estimates 40% of children aged 6-59 months, 37% of pregnant women and 30% of women aged 15-49 are anaemic — well below India's last measured rates.

An ambitious programme, measured by inputs

Anaemia Mukt Bharat, launched in 2018, combines prophylactic iron and folic acid supplementation, deworming, testing and treatment, behaviour-change communication, fortified food in public programmes and work on non-nutritional causes such as malaria. By March 2024, fortified rice containing iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 had replaced standard custom-milled rice across public safety-net programmes, and the government earmarked Rs 805.91 crore to states for nutritional interventions in 2024-25.

Those are input numbers: tablets supplied, rice fortified, money allocated. NFHS-6 still tracks some inputs, including mothers taking supplements for the recommended 100 to 180 days, and those figures have risen. What is missing is the outcome: haemoglobin in the population. As Poonam Muttreja of the Population Foundation of India put it, "What doesn't get counted also does not get done."

Why the test changed

The health ministry's reason is methodological, and it has substance. Earlier NFHS rounds used capillary blood from a finger prick. Squeezing the finger can mix in tissue fluid and dilute the sample, lowering the recorded haemoglobin and potentially overstating anaemia. Venous blood, drawn from a vein, is the clinical standard. The replacement survey, known as SAMPADA and previously as the Diet and Biomarkers Survey, was designed around venous sampling with a wider panel of diet and biomarker measures. Its fieldwork reportedly covered about 260,000 people in 183 districts and was completed in 2025.

The problem is the handover. A venous-based series cannot be read as a simple continuation of a capillary-based one. If the new survey reports a lower prevalence, no one will be able to say how much is real improvement and how much is the change of instrument without a published bridge or calibration study. Coverage is the second problem: 183 districts can support national and regional estimates, but NFHS could be cut by district across nearly 800 districts, which is the level at which a health official decides where to intensify testing and supplement distribution.

What happens next

Three things will determine whether this becomes a short gap or a long blind spot: how quickly the SAMPADA findings are released, whether the government publishes a method bridge to NFHS-5, and whether district-level monitoring is protected in the interim. Anaemia is also linked to folate and vitamin B12 deficiency, infections and inherited blood disorders, which is why a haemoglobin number tied to household data was so useful. Until the new series lands with its methods open, India's flagship anaemia programme will be judged on effort rather than results.
